newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt says PLO-Israel talks crucial for peace.
newsitem.headline: Egypt says PLO-Israel talks crucial for peace.

text.p: Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa said on Saturday that the Middle East would be thrown into a crisis if Israel does not change its hardline stance in Israeli-Palestinian negotiations starting on Sunday.

Speaking to reporters after a meeting between Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and Egypt's President Hosni Mubarak, Moussa said a pessimistic Middle East would scrutinise Sunday's talks on the Israeli border with the self-rule Gaza Strip and would take action if they turned out to be a waste of time.

"Pessimism is the prevailing feeling in the area. The Washington talks, the decision to resume negotiations, the presence of the American side... all that behooves the Israelis to move and change their negative posture," Moussa said.

"If not then it will be indeed be a very, very serious situation...our eyes are open and focussed on the negotiations and I don't think we will all keep quiet if they proved to be a waste of time or a farce," he added.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu held talks with Arafat on Tuesday and Wednesday in Washington to discuss their stalled peace process, with U.S. President Bill Clinton and Jordan's King Hussein present.

The meeting was aimed at ending the worst clashes between Israelis and Palestinians since a 1993 peace deal and pushing the Jewish state into fulfilling peace pledges it has delayed, like a redeployment from Hebron town in the West Bank.

The summit, deemed a failure by the Palestinans, Arabs and most of Europe, ended with both leaders agreeing on Sunday's talks. U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher will meet Netanyahu and Arafat but will not take part in the talks by aides of the two leaders.
Arafat held almost two hours of talks with Mubarak on Sunday's negotiations and on the Washington summit, which Mubarak refused to attend due to what he called Israeli intransigence.
"It's not a question of handshakes or summits that will change the situation. What will change the situation is a real move and a bona fide dealing with politics," Moussa added.
"The success of tomorrow's talks in implementing the agreements will be deemed a success of the Washington summit. Let us give these negotiations a chance," he said.

Moussa said the agenda of Sunday's talks had not been set yet but both sides are likely to discuss the closure of an archeological tunnel in Arab East Jerusalem -- its opening sparked the clashes in which 73 people died -- and troop withdrawl from Hebron, originally set to take place in March.

Netanyahu, who took office in June, has said he wants to renegotiate some parts of the Oslo peace accords, which called for the redeployment from Palestinian cities in the West Bank including Hebron, to ensure Israel's security. The other redeployments took place before Netanyahu won May elections.
The Palestinans refuse any adjustments of those treaties and Moussa said they would be unacceptable.
"Any Israeli change to the treaty is unfair and should not be taken into any sort of consideration," he said.
The Palestinian leader, who flew into Cairo after meeting French President Jacques Chirac in Paris and Italian leaders in Naples, has also called for a European presence in Sunday's talks.

In Dublin, Italy and France are pressing a one-day informal European Union summit to reaffirm the 15-nation bloc's desire to play a role in rescuing the Middle East peace process dominated by the mediation efforts of the United States.

Asked about Egypt's relations with Israel, Moussa said: "Relations are normal under the current circumstances. We are very upset with the Israeli politics and the Israeli way of handling the peace process but I would describe our relations as continuous relations."
